edges.source_hint: General chemistry textbooks' treatment of stoichiometry / the law of conservation of mass.
edges.rationale: Conservation of mass is a foundational quantitative law of chemistry, taught as a core principle in every general-chemistry curriculum; target field:chemistry is already reviewed.
edges.uncertainty: None expected beyond the node-level identity risk (none flagged for this node).

edges.source_hint: Encyclopedia Britannica 'Antoine Lavoisier'; general history-of-chemistry references on the law of conservation of mass.
edges.rationale: Lavoisier established the law of conservation of mass through systematic closed-vessel weighing experiments in the 1770s-1780s and stated it as a chemical principle in his 1789 Traite elementaire de chimie; this is the concept-level mirror of the existing reviewed edge from Lavoisier to field:chemistry.
edges.uncertainty: Confidence moderated for the Lomonosov priority question flagged at the node level: some sources (particularly Russian historiography) credit Mikhail Lomonosov with an earlier 1748-1756 statement and closed-vessel demonstration of the same principle, a genuine competing formalization claim rather than a vague precursor idea.

edges.source_hint: General biology textbooks' treatment of cell theory; Encyclopedia Britannica 'cell theory'.
edges.rationale: Cell theory is the founding unifying doctrine of cell biology as a discipline; target subfield:cell-biology is already reviewed.
edges.uncertainty: None beyond the node-level completeness question (Virchow's later addition is not represented).

edges.source_hint: Encyclopedia Britannica 'Theodor Schwann'; general history-of-biology references on cell theory's formulation.
edges.rationale: Schwann extended cell-based structure to animal tissue in Mikroskopische Untersuchungen (1839) and is standardly credited with synthesizing the unified cell theory covering both plant and animal life; concept-level mirror of the existing reviewed edge from Schwann to subfield:cell-biology.
edges.uncertainty: None major; standard, uncontested history-of-biology attribution.

edges.source_hint: Encyclopedia Britannica 'Matthias Jakob Schleiden'; general history-of-biology references on cell theory's formulation.
edges.rationale: Schleiden proposed that plant tissues are composed of cells in his 1838 essay Beitrage zur Phytogenesis, the paper that directly prompted Schwann's animal-tissue extension the following year; concept-level mirror of the existing reviewed edge from Schleiden to subfield:cell-biology.
edges.uncertainty: None major; standard, uncontested history-of-biology attribution, though Schleiden's own account of cell formation (which he believed involved crystallization-like processes) was later superseded -- this does not affect his credit for the plant-cell half of the founding claim.

edges.source_hint: Encyclopedia Britannica 'germ theory'; general history-of-medicine references.
edges.rationale: Germ theory of disease is the founding doctrine of microbiology as a medical/biological discipline; target subfield:microbiology is already reviewed.
edges.uncertainty: None beyond the node-level homonym-collision risk (addressed in the node's referent).

edges.source_hint: Encyclopedia Britannica 'Louis Pasteur'; general history-of-medicine references on germ theory.
edges.rationale: Pasteur's 1860s experiments disproving spontaneous generation and demonstrating microbial roles in fermentation and disease (e.g. silkworm disease, anthrax, rabies work) are standardly credited as founding the experimental case for germ theory; concept-level mirror of the existing reviewed edge from Pasteur to subfield:microbiology.
edges.uncertainty: None major; standard, uncontested history-of-medicine attribution.

edges.source_hint: Encyclopedia Britannica 'Robert Koch'; general history-of-medicine references on Koch's postulates.
edges.rationale: Koch's postulates (1884) and his identification of specific disease-causing bacteria (anthrax 1876, tuberculosis 1882, cholera 1883) formalized the causal criteria connecting specific microorganisms to specific diseases, completing germ theory's experimental/methodological formalization; concept-level mirror of the existing reviewed edge from Koch to subfield:microbiology.
edges.uncertainty: None major; standard, uncontested history-of-medicine attribution.

edges.source_hint: Encyclopedia Britannica 'uniformitarianism'; general history-of-geology references.
edges.rationale: Uniformitarianism is geology's founding methodological doctrine, historically opposed to catastrophism; target subfield:geology is already reviewed.
edges.uncertainty: None expected.

edges.source_hint: Encyclopedia Britannica 'James Hutton'; general history-of-geology references on uniformitarianism's origin.
edges.rationale: Hutton originated the uniformitarian principle in Theory of the Earth (1788/1795), arguing that present-day geological processes, given enough time, explain the Earth's rock record; concept-level mirror of the existing reviewed edge from Hutton to subfield:geology.
edges.uncertainty: None major; Hutton is the standard-credited originator, though his dense prose meant the idea only spread widely after Playfair's and later Lyell's more accessible restatements.

edges.source_hint: Encyclopedia Britannica 'Charles Lyell'; general history-of-geology references on Principles of Geology.
edges.rationale: Lyell's Principles of Geology (1830-1833) systematized and popularized uniformitarianism as geology's guiding methodological principle, and is standardly credited with establishing it as the discipline's dominant framework (and with directly influencing Darwin); concept-level mirror of the existing reviewed edge from Lyell to subfield:geology.
edges.uncertainty: None major; standard, uncontested history-of-geology attribution, and Lyell already has a reviewed canonical_work edge for Principles of Geology in this corpus.

edges.source_hint: General physics/thermodynamics textbooks' treatment of entropy and the second law; Encyclopedia Britannica 'entropy'.
edges.rationale: Entropy (the classical thermodynamic sense) is the central state function of the second law of thermodynamics; target subfield:thermodynamics is already reviewed.
edges.uncertainty: Confidence moderated for the node-level multi-sense identity risk (statistical-mechanical and information-theoretic 'entropy' are related but formally distinct concepts that could be conflated by a resolver).

edges.source_hint: Nobel Prize committee citation for Herbert Simon (1978); general behavioral-economics textbooks' treatment of bounded rationality as a founding concept.
edges.rationale: Bounded rationality is standardly presented as one of the founding concepts of behavioral economics (the critique of full rational-actor optimization); target subfield:behavioral-economics is already reviewed and is the more referent-precise of the two candidate homes the order offered.
edges.uncertainty: The candidate explicitly offered a second option, field:economics, since Simon's original 1940s-1950s work (Administrative Behavior, Models of Man) predates behavioral economics' formal establishment as a subfield by decades and was framed more broadly as organizational/administrative decision theory; QC should weigh whether field:economics is the more historically accurate part_of target instead.

edges.source_hint: Nobel Prize committee citation for Herbert Simon (1978); Encyclopedia Britannica 'Herbert A. Simon'.
edges.rationale: Simon coined and developed bounded rationality across Administrative Behavior (1947) and Models of Man (1957), and it is the concept most explicitly cited in his 1978 Nobel Prize in Economics citation; a clean, well-documented person-to-concept founding claim, his first economics-related edge in this corpus.
edges.uncertainty: foundry/rejections.json already records a declined Herbert Simon-to-thermodynamics probe from a different batch (an unrelated cross-disciplinary metaphor, correctly rejected there); this edge is a distinct, squarely-sourced claim about Simon's actual signature contribution, not a repeat of that pattern -- flagged explicitly so QC does not conflate the two.

edges.rationale: The ideal type is a foundational methodological concept of Weberian sociology and interpretive social science generally; target field:sociology is already reviewed.
edges.uncertainty: None beyond the node-level homonym-collision risk (addressed in the node's referent).

edges.source_hint: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy 'Max Weber'; general sociology-methods textbooks.
edges.rationale: Weber developed the ideal-type method explicitly in his methodological essays (notably 'Die Objektivitat sozialwissenschaftlicher und sozialpolitischer Erkenntnis', 1904) as his signature contribution to social-science method; concept-level companion to Weber's existing reviewed founding edge to field:sociology.
edges.uncertainty: None major; standard, uncontested history-of-sociology attribution.

edges.source_hint: General economics textbooks' treatment of Adam Smith and the division of labour; Encyclopedia Britannica 'division of labour'.
edges.rationale: Division of labour is one of the central organizing concepts of classical economics, opening Smith's Wealth of Nations; target field:economics is already reviewed.
edges.uncertainty: None beyond the node-level Durkheim-homonym risk (addressed in the node's referent) -- within economics specifically, the field-level attachment is not contested.

edges.source_hint: General economics textbooks' treatment of Adam Smith and the division of labour; Encyclopedia Britannica 'Adam Smith'.
edges.rationale: Smith gave division of labour its canonical modern economic treatment in the opening chapters of Wealth of Nations (1776), including the pin-factory example, establishing it as a central mechanism of economic growth; concept-level mirror of Smith's existing reviewed founding edge to field:economics, alongside the existing concept:invisible-hand (a distinct Smith concept about market coordination, not specialization).
edges.uncertainty: Confidence moderated for the node-level precursor question: Bernard Mandeville and William Petty discussed specialization before Smith, and the general idea traces back to ancient sources (Plato's Republic, Xenophon), so 'founded' reflects Smith's canonical systematic economic treatment, not the bare idea's origin.

edges.source_hint: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entries on set theory and on Georg Cantor; general set-theory textbooks' treatment of cardinality via bijection.
edges.rationale: Cardinality (the bijection-based size-comparison sense) is the core concept Cantor introduced to found set theory as a rigorous discipline; target subfield:set-theory is already reviewed.
edges.uncertainty: Confidence moderated for the node-level three-way referent risk carried over from the concept-wave2-v1 hold (cardinality vs. cardinal number vs. transfinite number); this is a re-examination, not a resolved question, given no live verification is available.

edges.source_hint: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy 'Georg Cantor'; general history-of-mathematics references on Cantor's cardinality results.
edges.rationale: Cantor introduced the comparison of infinite sets by cardinality (bijective correspondence) and proved that transfinite cardinals form a strict hierarchy (1874-1895, including the 1891 diagonal argument), the founding result of set theory; concept-level mirror of Cantor's existing reviewed founding edge to subfield:set-theory.
edges.uncertainty: Same node-level three-way referent risk as the sibling part_of edge; if QC or a resolver determines the corpus should instead carry 'cardinal number' or 'transfinite number' as the referent-precise node, this edge should be re-scoped to match rather than dropped, since the underlying founding claim (Cantor originating the size-comparison idea) is solid regardless of which of the three labels the corpus settles on.

edges.source_hint: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy 'Boole, George'; general mathematical-logic textbooks' treatment of Boolean algebra as a formal system for propositional logic.
edges.rationale: Boolean algebra, as the formal algebraic system Boole devised, provides a formal algebraic framing for propositional logic within mathematical logic -- matching `formalizes` ('A provides a formal mathematical/logical framing for B') more precisely than `part_of`, since the claim is about Boolean algebra formalizing logical reasoning rather than being a sub-area of the discipline itself; target subfield:mathematical-logic is already reviewed.
edges.uncertainty: This is a deliberate relation-choice departure from the concept-wave2-v1 draft of this same candidate, which used part_of; confidence set moderately given both the residual node-level referent risk (see node uncertainty) and genuine judgment-call risk in the relation choice itself -- QC may reasonably prefer part_of instead, mirroring the lambda-calculus/turing-machine precedent of formal-system concepts attaching to their subfield via part_of rather than formalizes.

edges.source_hint: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy 'Boole, George'; general history-of-logic references on The Laws of Thought.
edges.rationale: Boole introduced the algebraic system bearing his name in The Mathematical Analysis of Logic (1847) and The Laws of Thought (1854); concept-level mirror of Boole's existing reviewed founding edge to subfield:mathematical-logic.
edges.uncertainty: Same node-level referent risk as the sibling formalizes edge (see node uncertainty); the underlying founding claim (Boole originating the algebraic system) is solid regardless of how the identity question resolves.

edges.source_hint: General physics textbooks' treatment of special and general relativity; Encyclopedia Britannica 'relativity'.
edges.rationale: The theory of relativity is a foundational theory of modern physics; target field:physics is already reviewed.
edges.uncertainty: None expected; this edge is uncontested regardless of the founder-attribution question flagged at the node/sibling-edge level.

edges.source_hint: General history-of-physics references on the Einstein-Poincare-Lorentz relativity priority question; Encyclopedia Britannica 'Henri Poincare' and 'relativity'.
edges.rationale: Poincare's work on the electrodynamics of moving bodies (Sur la dynamique de l'electron, 1905/1906), his articulation of a relativity principle, his naming of the Lorentz transformation, and the group later called the Poincare group are well-documented, uncontroversial precursor/contemporaneous contributions that influenced the surrounding development of relativistic physics. `influenced` is used deliberately instead of `founded_or_formalized` because the mainstream-credited founder of the theory of relativity is Albert Einstein, not Poincare, and person:albert-einstein does not currently exist in this corpus -- using founded_or_formalized here would assert or imply the minority/disputed Einstein-Poincare priority position rather than the mainstream one.
edges.uncertainty: Confidence set moderately (not high) because even `influenced` risks being read as crediting Poincare more centrally than the mainstream historical record supports, especially since this batch cannot also add a competing, higher-confidence founded_or_formalized edge from Einstein (he is not a corpus node). QC should treat this concept as founder-incomplete until a future batch adds Einstein, and should weigh whether to hold this edge entirely (not just flag it) until that gap is closed, rather than let a single influenced edge stand as the concept's only person-level attachment in the meantime.

edges.source_hint: Encyclopedia Britannica 'Charles Darwin' and 'evolution'; general history-of-biology references on On the Origin of Species.
edges.rationale: Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859) gave the theory of evolution its first rigorous, evidence-backed scientific formulation and is standardly credited as founding the modern scientific theory of evolution; concept-level mirror of Darwin's existing reviewed founding edges to subfield:evolutionary-biology and concept:natural-selection.
edges.uncertainty: Confidence set below the node's other sibling edges for two compounding reasons already flagged at the node level: (1) evolutionary/transmutation ideas predate Darwin (Lamarck 1809, Erasmus Darwin, Chambers's 1844 Vestiges), so 'founded' reflects rigorous formalization rather than pure origination; (2) this edge duplicates the exact same endpoint pair and relation as the already-reviewed edge:charles-darwin-founded-natural-selection (same source, same relation, different but closely related target) -- QC should confirm concept:evolution and concept:natural-selection are genuinely distinct referents before promoting both founder edges, since if they collapse to one entity this edge would be a straightforward duplicate.
